lead: An engine cannot light fuel at standstill. A starter spins the compressor until airflow supports combustion; then ignition and fuel take over. This chapter covers air turbine and electric starters, exciters, start sequencing and abnormal starts. Only a few universities teach this in detail.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 for bleed air used by air starters, and Chapter 2.4 for the fuel that must be lit.

blocks.text: A starter is a motor that turns the HP compressor through the accessory gearbox. It supplies torque until self-sustaining speed. Cut-out is scheduled on N2, HP spool speed as a percentage of design speed, not fixed time.

An air turbine starter (ATS) is a small turbine driven by regulated bleed air. A start valve admits air from the APU, the other engine, or a ground cart. A reduction gear and clutch drive the gearbox; the clutch disengages at cut-out so the running engine cannot overspeed the starter. Cross-bleed starting takes air from a running engine; APU starting uses the auxiliary power unit.

An electric starter is a DC series motor, often a starter-generator: it cranks, then generates. A contactor and current limiter protect the supply. Electric starters suit small engines and APUs; large turbofans usually use air starters.

An exciter takes a low-voltage supply (28 V DC, or 115 V AC on some types, rectified inside). A capacitor stores charge, and a transformer raises it to a high-voltage pulse at the igniter plug. The plug is a spark gap in the combustor liner.

Low-energy ignition, a few joules, suits normal starts. High-energy ignition, tens of joules, gives a spark that survives rain, cold and lean mixtures. Two igniters give redundancy; some engines fire both for start.

Continuous ignition is selected in heavy rain, turbulence and on contaminated runways, so a flameout relights at once. It is also used in volcanic ash, though ash damages the engine. Igniters stay off in cruise to save plug life. The FADEC schedules ignition and fuel.
Low-energy systems use a smaller capacitor and cost less; high-energy systems are heavier but reliable in bad weather.

The crew selects START. The start valve opens or the starter contactor closes, and the starter cranks N2. Ignition is energised at about 15 % N2. Fuel opens later, at about 20 % N2, when airflow can support a stable mixture. Light-off raises EGT and N2 accelerates. At cut-out, typically 25-40 % N2 on the engines these notes cover, the starter disengages. Cut-out is engine-specific and always above self-sustaining speed; quote it only from the start schedule. The engine then accelerates to idle. In the timeline, starter cranks 0-20 s, igniters at 15 s, fuel at 20 s, light-off near 22 s, idle about 40 s.

Interlocks stop unsafe starts. The start valve will not open with low bleed pressure or if the engine is already rotating above a threshold. Fuel is inhibited below minimum N2. Ignition must be on before fuel. Cut-out must occur above self-sustaining speed.

A hot start is EGT beyond the start limit, from excess fuel or late ignition. A hung start is N2 stalling below idle, from weak starter or low bleed. Dry motoring turns the engine with fuel and ignition off to clear vapour or cool a hot start.

figure.caption: Start timeline: starter cranks 0 to 20 s, igniters at 15 s, fuel at 20 s, light-off near 22 s, idle around 40 s. Starter cut-out at 20 s comes before idle.

spec.aria: The starter cranks from 0 to 20 s, igniters come on at 15 s, fuel at 20 s, light-off near 22 s and the engine reaches idle by about 40 s.

examples.question: A start reaches 60 % N2 in 40 s, linear. Find (a) average acceleration, (b) N2 at 20 s, (c) margin if measured cut-out N2 is 25 % and self-sustaining speed is 20 % N2.
steps: Average acceleration = change in N2 divided by time = (60 - 0) % N2 / 40 s = 1.5 % N2 per second.
Predicted N2 at 20 s = 1.5 % N2/s × 20 s = 30 % N2.
Measured cut-out N2 is 25 %; self-sustaining speed is 20 %.
Margin = 25 - 20 = 5 percentage points. The measured spool is slower than predicted but still above self-sustaining speed.
examples.answer: Average acceleration is 1.5 % N2 per second; the linear prediction at 20 s is 30 % N2; measured cut-out N2 of 25 % leaves a 5 percentage-point margin over 20 % self-sustaining speed.
examples.check:
acc = (60 - 0) / 40
pred = acc * 20
margin = 25 - 20
print(acc)
print(pred)
print(margin)

traps: N1 is fan speed; the start schedule is on N2, the HP spool.
A hot start is EGT exceedance; a hung start is N2 stall. They differ.
Cut-out is triggered by N2, not clock time.
Fuel too early, or too much before N2 is high enough, gives a rich mixture and hot start. Ignition must be on before fuel, so early ignition is correct, not a fault.
Low- and high-energy ignition differ in spark energy; high energy does not mean more fuel.

quiz.a: The N2 above which the engine runs without starter help.

quiz.q: Why is fuel opened after ignition and above a minimum N2?
quiz.a: To have enough airflow for a stable mixture and avoid a rich mixture or hot start.

quiz.q: A start reaches 72 % N2 in 24 s. Find the average acceleration.
EGT rises sharply before N2 passes 20 %. Name the event and give the first action.
quiz.a: Hot start. Cut fuel; keep cranking or dry-motor to clear and cool the engine.

quiz.q: Name the two common starter types.
quiz.a: Air turbine starter and electric starter or starter-generator.

quiz.q: Why does the starter clutch disengage at cut-out?
quiz.a: So the running engine does not overspeed the starter.

quiz.q: A cross-bleed start hangs at 18 % N2. Give two likely causes.
quiz.a: Low bleed pressure or a faulty start valve; weak starter or high accessory load.

beyond: Not for the exam. FADEC automatic start sequencing watches N2, EGT and fuel flow and aborts hot or hung starts. Starter-generators are growing in more-electric aircraft: one machine cranks and later supplies DC. Health monitoring records start times and EGT peaks to predict starter or igniter wear.
